A1.justification: Both PDFs support comparison of text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Despite retitling and expansion, they share the authors, core method and original BridgeData experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original progress-estimation experiments in Table 1 and adaptation-strategy experiments in Appendix C, Table 3.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds scripted-trajectory discrimination, sampling ablations and offline reinforcement-learning results in Tables 2 and 4.

M1.justification: v2 narrows the proposed configuration to implicit-memory TTT-IM, renamed VITA, removing the explicit-window/reset TTT-EX option. The encoder, reconstruction loss, regression head and meta-learning core remain unchanged. The newly documented sampling heuristic does not establish that its implementation changed.

E1.justification: The original BridgeData coverage is retained. v2 adds four randomized-controller subsets for expert versus non-expert discrimination and Meta-World MT10 for simulated offline policy learning, extending both behavioral coverage and downstream task requirements.

E2.justification: The principal VLM comparators remain, with CLIP renamed VLM-CL, while TTT-EX disappears from Table 1. v2 adds META-WL as the native-reward comparator and full-trajectory/random sampling controls. GVL's offline-RL entries are unevaluated dashes; the Qwen and GPT-4o trials already appeared in v1 Appendix B.3.

E3.justification: v2 introduces BinVOC discrimination evaluation and an offline-IQL protocol using 20 demonstrations per task, 100,000 training steps and 20 evaluation rollouts per task with horizon 150. Appendix D.1 also changes the default sampled-window count from eight to sixteen, although Section 4.1 retains eight; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test expert-versus-scripted discrimination and the effects of full-trajectory, random and dissimilarity sampling, including window-length and window-count variations. The temporal-adaptation analysis in v1 Appendix C is retained in v2 Appendix F.2 with renamed methods and identical numerical results, rather than being a new ablation.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without repeated-run or uncertainty information. For its new offline-RL experiment, v2 reports ten seeds covering data generation and policy training, plus 95% confidence intervals from 10,000 task-stratified bootstrap resamples. The retained VOC experiments still lack uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds BinVOC, sampling-ablation and offline-RL results; Table 2 reports VITA's IQM as 0.815 versus META-WL's 0.779. Original VOC results mostly change only by rounding, but GVL-1S on dt_tk_pnp changes from 0.2151 to 0.211, and TTT-EX entries are removed. Table 4's full-trajectory average of 0.25 conflicts with its two successful cases out of four.

T1.justification: v2 adds the diversity-score/top-k formulation in Equation 5, the BinVOC indicator definition and a sampling-complexity derivation in Appendix G. Core value and reconstruction-loss definitions are retained; the latter already appeared in v1 Figure 1. No shortcut-learning theorem is added, and Appendix G's numerical cost estimate contains an arithmetic error.

C1.justification: The original distribution-shift generalization claim remains. v2 adds a central claim that value estimates trained on real-world trajectories support zero-shot simulated reward shaping and yield offline policies outperforming Meta-World's dense rewards. Expert-versus-non-expert discrimination also becomes an explicitly claimed capability.

C2.justification: v2 develops new interpretations linking sampling diversity to reduced redundant-frame shortcuts and explaining real-to-simulation reward transfer. It qualifies scripted trajectories as lacking quantified suboptimality and adds limitations involving execution variability, long durations and deployment-time updates. These substantially extend v1's brief discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds concrete IQL/d3rlpy hyperparameters, training and evaluation schedules, generic descriptions for unannotated scripted data, and batched GPU distance computation for sampling. Most original encoder, optimizer and hardware details are retained. Reproducibility remains limited by ambiguous sampling defaults and the absence of an explicit value-to-reward construction.

R1.justification: A substantial Related Work section newly positions VITA against RoboCLIP, ReWiND, Video-Language Critic, DecisionNCE and prompt-based adaptation. The introduction also expands discussion of world models and latent-action learning, substantially broadening v1's shorter inline research positioning.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around VITA and zero-shot value functions. v1's compact organization becomes separate preliminaries, expanded method and experiment subsections, related work, and discussion with limitations and future work. Existing appendix material is regrouped alongside additions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, and Figure 1 is redrawn around training and inference. v2 adds a main-text trajectory gallery, scripted examples, a two-panel results table and a sampling-ablation table. Existing appendix illustrations are retained, while the dataset table replaces shift checkmarks with embodiment names.

improvement.justification: The new sampling ablations directly test a central component that v1 did not isolate experimentally. Scripted-trajectory checks and ten-seed offline-RL experiments substantially strengthen evidence beyond expert-trajectory rank correlation, with useful uncertainty and implementation reporting. These gains outweigh the new reporting weaknesses, including Table 4's inconsistent average and Appendix G's cost arithmetic. The overlapping RL confidence intervals and incomplete reward-construction details nevertheless qualify the strength and reproducibility of the claimed downstream superiority.
